learn.intro: Some jobs need the same quick judgment thousands of times: which team should handle this support ticket? Jev and an LLM both read the ticket and pick one of the same five teams.

compare.title: Jev, a System One model
points: Answers a typed question: here, a choice of one team
Returns the answer as data, with no text to write
Charges only for the tokens it reads

compare.title: An LLM, a System Two model
points: Reads the same ticket and the same five teams
Writes its answer as text, in a fixed JSON format
Charges for the tokens it reads and the tokens it writes

questions.prompt: Who sorts all the tickets first?

why: Jev returns a typed answer with no text to write, and pays only for the tokens it reads. The LLM writes its answer as text and pays for every token it writes, on every ticket.

On accuracy the race is close, and it depends on the opponent: check the Accuracy column above. An LLM that writes anything around its JSON can't be parsed, so that answer counts as a miss even when the right team is inside it.
One ticket makes little difference. Thousands of tickets a day is where speed and cost add up.

questions.prompt: Your shop gets 50,000 support tickets a day, and each one needs one of five teams. Which tool fits this job best?

options.text: Jev: one typed Choice per ticket, fast and cheap at scale
An LLM: it writes a reasoned answer for every ticket
Plain Code: keyword rules always pick the right team

questions.explanation: Routing a ticket is one quick judgment repeated many times. Jev answers each with a typed Choice, so it is fast and pays only for the tokens it reads. Keyword rules break on wording they don't expect.

questions.prompt: Why did the LLM cost more per ticket in the race?

options.text: It pays for the tokens it writes, not only the ones it reads
It got tickets wrong and had to try them again
It was asked more questions per ticket

questions.explanation: Both read the same ticket and the same five teams, with one request per ticket and no retries. The LLM also writes its answer as text, and every token it writes is billed. Jev returns the answer as data and pays only for what it reads.
